passage: The colony's Saturday football match in Dwarka was short one player, and Anand, captain as usual, looked over the boys by the gate. The new boy from B-block spoke slow Hindi with a Malayalam accent and carried a physics book. "He'll be useless," Anand muttered to Disha. "Nerd type." He picked a tall boy with spiky hair instead, who looked like he played. Disha rolled her eyes and put the new boy on her team. In twenty minutes the new boy had scored twice, weaving past Anand as if he wasn't there. The tall boy missed three easy passes. At half-time Anand walked over, red-faced. "Where did you learn to play like that?" "School team, back home in Kozhikode," the boy said.

qa.q: How many goals did the new boy score in twenty minutes?
qa.a: The new boy scored twice in twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel sure the new boy would be useless?
qa.a: The accent and the physics book matched Anand's idea of a nerd type, and the tall spiky-haired boy looked like a player, so the match to a type felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Anand try as captain next time?
qa.a: He could ask new players what they play and watch a few minutes of passing before choosing, instead of picking by looks or accent.

qa.q: How might the new boy have felt when Anand called him useless?
qa.a: If he heard it, he may have felt dismissed and eager to prove himself, and scoring twice probably felt satisfying.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a new boy's football skill from his accent and a physics book, and being surprised by the game.

"That new boy in tuition has an earring and ripped jeans," Pradeep said, reaching for the rice. "He's obviously the trouble type."
"Obviously?" his cousin Chaitanya asked. "Did he do anything?"
"No, but you can tell. And the girl who sits in front, the one who talks so softly? Topper. Definitely."
"Based on?"
"Based on... she has neat handwriting."
Mausi laughed from the kitchen. "And what did the test say?"
Pradeep went quiet. "The earring guy got the highest marks. The soft-spoken girl failed."
"So?" Chaitanya grinned.
"So... it was a weird test," Pradeep said, but he was frowning into his plate.
"Or," said Chaitanya, "maybe you can't tell."

qa.q: What did the test show about the boy with the earring?
qa.a: The earring guy got the highest marks.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep call it a weird test?
qa.a: Pradeep feels uncomfortable because the results clash with the types he had in his head, and blaming the test lets him keep those guesses. His frown suggests he half suspects he was wrong.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do the next time he forms a quick judgment about a classmate?
qa.a: He could ask himself what he has actually seen the person do, and wait for real evidence, like marks or behaviour, before labelling them.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya keep asking short questions instead of lecturing?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems to want Pradeep to notice the gap himself; questions like "Based on?" let the facts do the arguing without starting a fight.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy deciding who is trouble and who is a topper from looks and voice, then being surprised when the test disagrees.

passage: When I was in class nine, I thought I could read people like a scoreboard. My name is Pranav, and I was the kid who sorted everyone in the first week. Vidya was small, wore thick glasses and spoke so softly that the teacher kept asking her to repeat. So in my head she went into a box: bookish, bad at sports. When we were put in the same relay team for sports day, I groaned out loud. Then in practice she ran the third leg and overtook two runners. It turned out she had been training for district athletics since she was ten. I remember standing there with the baton, feeling stupid. I'd been so sure. It had felt exactly like knowing.

qa.q: Which leg of the relay did Vidya run?
qa.a: Vidya ran the third leg and overtook two runners.

qa.q: Why did Pranav groan when put in Vidya's relay team?
qa.a: Her small size, thick glasses and soft voice fitted Pranav's box of bookish and bad at sports, so the guess felt like knowing.

qa.q: What could Pranav tell a younger student who sorts people in the first week?
qa.a: That a first-week guess from looks or voice is only a guess; wait to see what people actually do, like how they run in practice, before deciding.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt hearing Pranav groan?
qa.a: Vidya may have felt hurt or underestimated, and perhaps quietly determined to show what she could do in practice.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a classmate as bad at sports from her size, glasses and soft voice, and being surprised by the relay.

passage:
Teacher's note: Class 9 chemistry, practical lab, 12 August. Written by Nikita Sharma.
Today I let students pick lab partners for the titration practical. Gautam, usually thoughtful, avoided Birsa, the tall boy who joined on the sports quota. I heard Gautam tell his friend, "He's a footballer, he won't know titration." He chose the student with the neatest notebook instead. During the practical, Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times. Birsa and his partner got a clean result on the first try, and Birsa explained the colour change to the next table. Gautam watched with his mouth half open. After class he came to my desk and said, "Ma'am, I thought he'd be bad at this. I was wrong." We talked about how he had decided before seeing any evidence. Next week I'll rotate partners at random, and I've asked Gautam to work with Birsa.

qa.q: What happened to Gautam's pair during the practical?
qa.a: Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times.

qa.q: Why did it seem sensible to Gautam that Birsa wouldn't know titration?
qa.a: Gautam felt confident because Birsa was tall and joined on the sports quota, which fit his idea of a footballer, not a chemist. The match to a type felt like enough reason.

qa.q: What did Nikita decide to do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: She will rotate partners at random and has asked Gautam to work with Birsa, so Gautam can learn about Birsa from real work instead of assumptions.

qa.q: What might it be like for Birsa to be overlooked as a lab partner?
qa.a: Birsa may be used to people assuming sports is all he is good at, and explaining the colour change to the next table may have felt like a quiet way of proving otherwise.

grounding: A teacher notes that a teenage boy avoided a sports-quota classmate as a lab partner, assuming he'd be weak, and was surprised by his skill.

passage:
Friday, 9 pm
Diary, I owe someone an apology, but only in here.
The new girl, Indu, joined our class last week. She has heavy kajal, loud bangles, and she talks back to teachers in a way that makes everyone gasp. So on day one I told Ronit, "Trouble. You'll see. She'll be in the principal's office in a month." And every time she laughed in class I thought, see?
Today I lost my wallet in the canteen. It had my bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave me. I was panicking. Then Indu came up and handed it to me. "Found it under the bench. Count it." Everything was there.
I just stood there like a fool and said thanks. I had her figured out completely wrong, and I didn't even know her.
Mummy says a good son says sorry properly. Maybe Monday.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What was in Vaibhav's wallet?
qa.a: His bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave him.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel sure that Indu was trouble?
qa.a: Her kajal, bangles and way of talking back matched his idea of a troublemaker, so every laugh in class seemed to confirm it.

qa.q: What choice is Vaibhav thinking about for Monday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Saying sorry properly to Indu. It would mean acting on what he learned from what she did, not on his first judgement.

qa.q: How might Indu feel if she knew Vaibhav had called her trouble on day one?
qa.a: She might feel hurt or unsurprised, if people often judge her by her look, and his apology could mean a lot to her.

grounding: A teenage boy's diary shows he judged a new girl as trouble from her looks and speech, and was surprised when she returned his lost wallet.

passage: At the kasba high school in Nanded district, Irawati's group needed a fourth member for the maths model. "Not her," Irawati whispered, nodding at Kavitha, the new girl from the hill village, who said "ho-ji" to teachers and whose Marathi had a thick village lilt. "She'll be slow. Take Ruchika, she talks like a news reader." Ruchika joined and spent two days making the chart pretty. On the third day, with the model due, their pyramid kept collapsing. Kavitha, walking past with her tiffin, stopped. "Your base angles are wrong. Here." She took a pencil, did the sums in the margin in under a minute, and the pyramid stood. Irawati's mouth hung open. "How did you...?" "My father builds houses," said Kavitha. "Angles are dinner talk."

qa.q: What was wrong with the group's pyramid?
qa.a: Its base angles were wrong, so it kept collapsing.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel so sure Kavitha would be slow?
qa.a: She felt sure and a little superior, because Kavitha's village accent and polite ho-ji matched her picture of a weak student, so the match felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Irawati do next time the group chooses a member?
qa.a: Ask people what they're good at, or look at their actual work, instead of choosing by how they speak.

qa.q: What might it be like for Kavitha to be passed over and then fix the model?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt left out at first, then calm and quietly proud when her sums made the pyramid stand.

grounding: A teenager judges a new girl as weak at maths from her village accent and is surprised when she solves the problem.

passage: When Mr Duarte announced that each class in their Lisbon school would pick a mentor for the fifth graders' reading club, Beatriz ruled Jamal out at once. Tall, hood always up, earphones in, slang in every sentence: the type who ends up outside the head's office. "He'll scare them," she told her friend, and volunteered herself instead. On Thursday Jamal came along only because the library was warm. Within ten minutes, Beatriz's group of ten-year-olds was fidgeting, and Jamal's was silent, leaning in, as he did the voices of three pirates. One small girl wouldn't let go of his sleeve at the end. "I read to my little brothers every night," he said, shrugging, when Beatriz stared. She walked home turning it over, slightly embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Jamal do to hold the children's attention?
qa.a: He did the voices of three pirates.

qa.q: Why was Beatriz so surprised by Jamal in the library?
qa.a: She was surprised, and a little embarrassed, because his hood, earphones and slang had seemed like proof he was trouble, yet he was the best reader there.

qa.q: What could Beatriz try before ruling someone out next time?
qa.a: Give the person a chance to show what they can do, or ask them, instead of deciding from clothes and slang.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel if he knew why Beatriz ruled him out?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and judged, since he reads to his little brothers every night and was dismissed for his hood and slang.

grounding: A teenager decides a classmate is trouble from his clothes and slang, and is surprised when he is the best reader with young children.

passage: At the district sports hostel in Kottayam, Elizabeth was picking the relay team for the inter-hostel meet. Siddharth, the new boy, was thin, spoke softly and carried a physics book everywhere. "Nerds don't sprint," she said to Coach, and put him down as reserve. Coach only nodded. "Time trials Saturday, then." On Saturday, the stopwatch said what Elizabeth didn't want to hear: Siddharth ran the hundred faster than two of her chosen runners, and his baton change was the cleanest on the track. She looked at her list, then at him, retying his laces as if it was nothing. "Why didn't you say?" she asked. "You didn't ask," he said, not unkindly. She tore up the list and wrote a new one from the times.

qa.q: What did the time trials show about Siddharth?
qa.a: He ran the hundred faster than two of her chosen runners, with the cleanest baton change on the track.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth put Siddharth down as reserve?
qa.a: She felt sure a thin, soft-spoken boy with a physics book could not sprint, so matching him to a type felt like enough evidence.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, and why?
qa.a: The time trials, because they judged every runner on real speed instead of on how they looked.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt being put down as reserve?
qa.a: He may have felt quietly overlooked but calm, trusting the stopwatch to show what he could do.

grounding: A teen captain assumes a quiet boy with a physics book cannot sprint and is surprised when the time trials say otherwise.

passage:
Dear Baljeet,

New school update. On the first day, I decided who everyone was. The tall boy with the basketball shoes: sports captain, bad at studies. The girl who speaks softly in Tamil-accented English: maths genius. The guy with the earring and the loud laugh: trouble, stay away.

Guess what? Three weeks later, the tall boy tops in chemistry and can't even dribble. The soft-spoken girl hates maths and runs the drama club. And the earring guy, Rizwan, is the one who helped me find the library and lent me his notes when I was sick.

I felt so sure on day one. It really felt like I could tell just by looking. Now I feel a bit embarrassed. I wonder how many people I've guessed wrong before.

Write back soon.

Farhan

qa.q: Who lent Farhan notes when Farhan was sick?
qa.a: Rizwan, the earring guy.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel so sure on the first day?
qa.a: Each person seemed to match a familiar type, so the match felt like proof; now Farhan feels surprised and a bit embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Farhan do differently with the next new people?
qa.a: Farhan could hold first guesses loosely and wait to see what people actually do before deciding who they are.

qa.q: How might Rizwan feel if he knew Farhan first thought he was trouble?
qa.a: Rizwan might feel hurt or amused, having been kind despite the unfair first judgement.

grounding: It shows a teenager who judges classmates' abilities from how they look or speak and is surprised when reality disagrees.

passage: Nitin, you asked why I changed seats in maths class. Okay, so here's the story. When I joined the new school in Class 9, I sat next to the boy who wore thick glasses and carried three geometry boxes. I thought, this guy's obviously a maths genius, I'll learn from him. And I avoided the boy from the hockey team who always joked around, because I thought, sports types don't do maths. Then the first test came. Glasses boy got thirty-five out of a hundred. Hockey boy, Joel, got ninety-eight. I literally stared at the list for a whole minute. I was so surprised. It felt like my brain had lied to me. So I asked Joel if I could sit with him. He laughed and said, "You thought I was dumb, didn't you?" I said sorry. Now he explains trigonometry better than the teacher. That's Vaibhav's lesson.

qa.q: What did the hockey boy score in the first test?
qa.a: Ninety-eight.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel sure about the glasses boy and the hockey boy?
qa.a: Each matched a familiar type, so it felt obvious, and the results left Vaibhav very surprised, as if the brain had lied.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do after seeing the results, and why was it good?
qa.a: Vaibhav apologised to Joel and asked to sit with him, choosing based on real evidence instead of looks.

qa.q: How did Joel seem to react when Vaibhav asked to sit with him?
qa.a: Joel seemed amused and guessed the unfair judgement, but was generous enough to help anyway.

grounding: It shows a teenager who decides who is good at maths from how people look and is surprised when reality disagrees.

June, first week. Shalini joined Imran's Class 11 in Lucknow from a village school. She wore oiled plaits and spoke Hindi with a rural accent. Imran decided at once: she'd be weak at science. When the teacher paired them for the physics project, he groaned. "She won't know anything."

July, a Wednesday. During the project, Shalini quietly corrected Imran's circuit diagram. He thought it was luck. She explained why his resistor was in the wrong place. He said nothing.

August, a Monday. The first term results went up. Shalini topped physics. Imran stood in front of the board, cheeks hot. He thought about the groan, the look he had given her. He went to find her. "Your diagram was right. I was... I thought you wouldn't know." Shalini smiled a little. "People always think that." Imran felt a sting of surprise at how many times she must have heard it.

qa.q: Where did Shalini come from?
qa.a: A village school.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he saw Shalini top physics?
qa.a: Imran felt surprised and embarrassed, cheeks hot, as he realised how unfair his first judgement had been.

qa.q: What could Imran do to avoid such snap judgements?
qa.a: He could notice when someone's look or accent triggers a guess, and wait for real evidence like their work before deciding.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to be underestimated?
qa.a: Shalini seems used to it, saying 'people always think that', which suggests she has faced this judgement many times.

grounding: It shows a teenager who judges a classmate's science ability by her accent and appearance, and is surprised when reality disagrees, over several months.

Trisha, you said the new girl looks like trouble? Hmm. Sit. Your Sabina khala has a story.

When I was fifteen, a girl called Rukhsar joined our school in Bhopal. She had short hair, rolled-up sleeves, a scar on her chin. She walked like she owned the corridor. I decided she was trouble. I told my friends to stay away.

Then the school's science exhibition came. My project on solar cookers kept failing. The mirrors wouldn't angle. I was nearly in tears. And who came over? Rukhsar. She fixed it in ten minutes. Her father was a welder; she'd been building things since she was six.

The scar was from a cycling fall.

I was so surprised I couldn't speak. My whole idea of her had come from how she looked.

So, Trisha, before you decide about this girl, what has she actually done?

qa.a: My project on solar cookers.

qa.q: What did young Sabina feel when Rukhsar fixed the project?
qa.a: Young Sabina felt so surprised she couldn't speak, and later realised her idea of Rukhsar came only from her looks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sabina's story?
qa.a: When Rukhsar came over and fixed the failing solar cooker, it showed Sabina that looks had told her nothing about who Rukhsar was.

qa.q: How might Rukhsar have felt when young Sabina's friends kept away?
qa.a: Rukhsar may have felt lonely and judged in a new school, yet she still chose to help.

The inter-school maths quiz was in twenty minutes, and their third teammate had phoned in sick. The teacher sent Simran, a Class 10 girl from the kabaddi team, to fill in.

Zubin groaned inside. Simran had a village accent, a sports jersey and scratched knees. Kabaddi girl, he thought. We're finished.

In the waiting room, he didn't even explain the rules to her. He just told her to write down answers if he asked.

The first round went badly. Zubin froze on a geometry question. Simran leaned over and whispered, "Isn't it 42? The triangle's isosceles." It was 42.

In the final round, Simran solved the probability question while the other schools were still scribbling. They came second.

On the bus back, Zubin sat quietly. He had matched her to a type: sporty, small town, not a maths person. The match had felt like proof.

qa.q: What answer did Simran whisper for the geometry question?
qa.a: Isn't it 42? The triangle's isosceles.

qa.q: Why was Zubin so sure Simran would be no help?
qa.a: Zubin felt certain and a bit dismissive, because Simran's accent, jersey and kabaddi team matched his idea of someone who isn't good at maths.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Zubin treated Simran, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Zubin didn't even explain the rules; next time he could treat a new teammate as capable and find out what they can do.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when Zubin didn't explain the rules?
qa.a: Simran might have felt dismissed and underestimated, but she still helped the team.

grounding: Under pressure before a quiz, a teenager judges a sporty teammate as weak at maths from her looks and is proved wrong.

On the first day of football trials in Bengaluru, Madhav watched the new boy, Jatin, walk onto the ground. Thin arms, glasses taped at the side, a science textbook still sticking out of his bag.

"He'll be last in the sprint," Madhav told his friend. "Bookworm."

Madhav then pointed at another boy, broad and loud, laughing at the edge. "That one's the striker. Look at him."

The coach blew the whistle. The broad boy tripped over the ball twice. Jatin, meanwhile, moved like water. He dribbled past two defenders, looked up, and passed perfectly. In the practice match he set up three goals.

Madhav stood with his mouth open.

After trials, Jatin said shyly that he'd played every evening in his old colony, usually against older boys.

Madhav felt stupid. He had picked the striker and the bookworm from their shapes and a textbook, and the field had shown him something completely different.

qa.q: How many goals did Jatin set up in the practice match?
qa.a: In the practice match he set up three goals.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel stupid after the trials?
qa.a: Madhav felt foolish and surprised because he had judged Jatin and the broad boy by their looks, and the game showed the opposite.

qa.q: What could Madhav do differently at the next trial?
qa.a: Madhav could wait until he has seen people play before deciding who is good.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel if he heard Madhav call him a bookworm?
qa.a: Jatin might feel hurt and underestimated, but proud that his play spoke for itself.

grounding: A teenager judges who will be good at football from body shape and glasses, and is surprised when the reverse is true.
